Rate Limiting

Two express-rate-limit instances — a generous one on every route, a tight one on /auth — the same idea as Laravel's throttle middleware.

If you've used Laravel's throttle middleware, express-rate-limit is the same idea: cap how many requests one client can make in a time window, reject the rest with a 429 Too Many Requests until the window resets. This project uses two separately-configured limiters rather than one blanket rule, because "how many requests is too many" is genuinely different for different routes:

// Figure 6.16: two limiters (src/middleware/rateLimiter.js)
export const generalLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 300,
  standardHeaders: true,
  legacyHeaders: false,
});

export const authLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 10,
  standardHeaders: true,
  legacyHeaders: false,
});

generalLimiter is a generous backstop against something going seriously wrong — a runaway client, a scraper — applied to every route in app.js, right alongside helmet/cors. authLimiter is deliberately far tighter, and applied only to /auth/register and /auth/login:

// Figure 6.17: routes/auth.routes.js
router.post('/register', authLimiter, validate({ body: registerSchema }), authController.register);
router.post('/login', authLimiter, validate({ body: loginSchema }), authController.login);

Login and register are the one place in this API where hammering an endpoint can actually profit an attacker — credential stuffing, brute-forcing a password — in a way that requesting the ticket list too often never does. Ten attempts per fifteen minutes is tight enough to make that impractical without locking out a real user who just mistyped their password a couple of times. standardHeaders: true is what put the RateLimit-* headers you'd see on any response — RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining — there for a client to actually see how close it is to being cut off, rather than finding out only once it gets a 429.
